text.p: The world faces a future of "increasingly complex and perverse ethical dilemmas" in healthcare over the next decade, one of Britain's leading drugs researchers warned on Wednesday.

George Poste, chairman of research and development at British-based drugs giant SmithKline Beecham Plc, said progress in the understanding of the make-up of the human body and the ability to predict and diagnose disease "will grow dramatically over the next decade, and with it will come a complex array of ethical and social questions."

In a speech to the annual business outlook conference of the Chemical Industries Association he said rapid advances in understanding human genes opened up the prospect of greatly improved disease management.
But he also warned that "public expectation is far outstripping the capacity of any OECD nation to provide healthcare" and said rationing of scarce resources "will become a way of life".
Poste predicted that progress in computing meant that each individual's health history and genetic propensity to disease would one day be held on "smart cards".
Genetic knowledge would allow those funding healthcare to target drugs and other forms of therapy at those best able to respond.

And he said molecular diagnostics also held out the prospect of discovering illness at much earlier stages and "if one can determine disease earlier it is better for the patient and for the healthcare system," said Poste.

But he said the ability to detect a genetic propensity for an illness like cancer will throw up complex dilemmas, particualrly if such information starts to be used to deny some people health insurance of mortgages.

Citing recent controversy in the U.S. about tests which purportedy reveal women with a higher natural risk of breast cancer, Poste said there was also a danger of creating a raft of "the worried well", and suicides among those who were wrongly made to fear a disease because of their genetic breakdown.
"The issues are profound. Health is a very tangible entity that transcends social, economic or educational background," Poste told the conference.
